source.title: Solutions to open problems in Neeb's recent survey on infinite-dimensional Lie groups

accepted.question_text: Does every subgroup H of an infinite-dimensional Lie group G admit a smooth manifold structure making H an initial Lie subgroup of G? Here a subgroup H is an initial Lie subgroup if H can be made into a Lie group, the inclusion map lambda: H -> G is C^k for every differentiability class k in N union {infinity}, every map f: X -> H from a C^k-manifold X is C^k whenever lambda composed with f is C^k, and the induced tangent map L(lambda): L(H) -> L(G) is injective.

evidence.quote: We describe a subgroup of an infinite-dimensional Lie group which is not an initial Lie subgroup (Section 1). This answers [21, Problem II.6], the "Initial Subgroup Problem," in the negative.

Definition 1.1 Let N := {1, 2, . . .}, k ∈ N ∪ {∞} and M be a C k -manifold. A subset N ⊆ M is called a C k -initial submanifold of M if N can be made a C k -manifold with the following properties: (a) The inclusion map λ : N → M is a C k -map; and (b) If X is a C k -manifold and f : X → N a map such that λ ◦ f is C k , then f is C k .

Following [21, Definition II.6.1], we say that a subgroup H ⊆ G is an initial Lie subgroup if it can be given a smooth manifold structure which makes H a Lie group, is C k -initial in G for each k ∈ N ∪ {∞}, and gives rise to an injective tangent map L(λ) := T1 (λ) : L(H) → L(G).
Theorem 1.3 For each k ∈ N ∪ {∞}, the additive subgroup N := ℓ∞ of bounded sequences is not a C k -initial submanifold of M := RN . In particular, it is not an initial Lie subgroup.

accepted.question_text: Let G_1 subseteq G_2 subseteq ... be finite-dimensional real Lie groups whose inclusion maps G_n -> G_{n+1} are smooth homomorphisms, and let G be their direct-limit Lie group. For every subgroup H of G, can H be made into an initial Lie subgroup of G? More explicitly, if H_n is G_n intersect H and H is given the direct-limit Lie group structure from the finite-dimensional Lie groups H_n, is the inclusion H -> G C^k-initial for every k in N union {infinity}, so that maps into H are C^k exactly when their composites into G are C^k, and does the tangent inclusion L(H) -> L(G) embed the Lie algebra of H into the Lie algebra of G?
accepted.context_brief: Subgroups of direct limit Lie groups

evidence.quote: We show that every subgroup of a direct limit G = lim−→ Gn of finite-dimensional Lie groups is an initial Lie subgroup (Section 2). This answers [21, Problem VII.3] in the affirmative.

Definition 1.1 Let N := {1, 2, . . .}, k ∈ N ∪ {∞} and M be a C k -manifold. A subset N ⊆ M is called a C k -initial submanifold of M if N can be made a C k -manifold with the following properties: (a) The inclusion map λ : N → M is a C k -map; and (b) If X is a C k -manifold and f : X → N a map such that λ ◦ f is C k , then f is C k .

Theorem 2.1 Let G1 ⊆ G2 ⊆ · · · be finite-dimensional Lie groups, such that the inclusion map Gn → Gn+1 is a smooth homomorphism for each n ∈ N. Let G = lim−→ Gn be the direct limit Lie group, and H ⊆ G be a subgroup. Equip Hn := Gn ∩ H with the finite-dimensional real Lie group structure induced by Gn and H with the Lie group structure making it the direct limit Lie group H = lim−→ Hn. Then the manifold structure on H is strongly C k -initial in G, for all k ∈ N ∪ {∞}. Thus H is an initial Lie subgroup of G.
The final conclusion is possible because the inclusion map λ : H → G gives rise to an embedding L(λ) : L(H) → L(G) by [7, Proposition 7.2].

accepted.question_text: Let G_1 subseteq G_2 subseteq ... be finite-dimensional Lie groups with smooth inclusion homomorphisms, and let G be their direct-limit Lie group. Is G a topological group with Lie algebra in the following sense: the space Hom_c(R,G) of continuous homomorphisms from the additive real line to G, equipped with the compact-open topology, has scalar multiplication (r gamma)(t)=gamma(tr), has addition given by (gamma+eta)(t)=lim_{n->infinity}(gamma(t/n) eta(t/n))^n, admits a continuous bilinear Lie bracket determined by the commutator-limit condition [gamma,eta](t^2)=lim_{n->infinity}(gamma(t/n) eta(t/n) gamma(-t/n) eta(-t/n))^{n^2}, and is naturally homeomorphic as a Lie algebra to L(G)?
accepted.context_brief: Direct limits as topological groups with Lie algebra

evidence.quote: We show that every direct limit G = lim−→ Gn of finite-dimensional Lie groups is a topological group with Lie algebra in the sense of [16] (Section 3). This answers [21, Problem VII.2] in the affirmative.

Given a (Hausdorff) topological group G, let C(R, G) be the set of continuous G-valued functions on R, and Homc (R, G) be the subset of all continuous homomorphisms from (R, +) to G. We equip C(R, G) and Homc (R, G) with the compact-open topology. Given r ∈ R and γ ∈ Homc (R, G), we define rγ ∈ Homc (R, G) via (rγ)(t) := γ(tr) for t ∈ R.

Definition 3.1 G is called a topological group with Lie algebra if (a) (γ + η)(t) := limn→∞ (γ(t/n)η(t/n))n exists for all γ, η ∈ Homc (R, G), and maps γ + η : R → G so obtained are continuous homomorphisms; (b) Homc (R, G) is a topological vector space with the addition defined in (a) and the scalar multiplication (8); and (c) There exists a continuous bilinear map [., .] : Homc (R, G) × Homc (R, G) → Homc (R, G) making it a Lie algebra, and such that [γ, η](t2 ) = limn→∞ (γ(t/n)η(t/n)γ(−t/n)η(−t/n))n2, for all γ, η ∈ Homc (R, G) and t ∈ R.
Theorem 3.4 For each direct limit Lie group G = lim−→ Gn as in 3.3, the mapping ΓG : L(G) → Homc (R, G) is a homeomorphism and thus G is a topological group with Lie algebra.

accepted.question_text: Let M be a sigma-compact finite-dimensional smooth manifold of dimension n > 0, let p be a point of M, and let Diff_c(M)_{p,0} be the subgroup of compactly supported smooth diffeomorphisms of M that fix p and whose tangent map at p has positive determinant. Let G_f^n(R)_0 be the group of formal diffeomorphisms of R^n whose linear part has positive determinant. After choosing a local chart phi around p with phi(p)=0, is every element of G_f^n(R)_0 realized as the Taylor series at 0 of phi composed with gamma composed with phi^{-1}, for some gamma in Diff_c(M)_{p,0}? Equivalently, is the Taylor-series homomorphism T_p^infinity: Diff_c(M)_{p,0} -> G_f^n(R)_0 surjective?

evidence.quote: Moreover, we prove a result by the author announced in [21], which answers a question posed in an earlier, unpublished version of the survey.

Let M be σ-compact finite-dimensional smooth manifold of dimension n > 0, and Diff c (M) be the Lie group of smooth diffeomorphisms γ : M → M which are compactly supported in the sense that the closure of {x ∈ M : γ(x) 6= x} is compact

Given p ∈ M, let Diff c (M)p be its stabilizer, and Diff c (M)p,0 be the subgroup of all γ ∈ Diff c (M)p such that det Tp (γ) > 0, where Tp (γ) : Tp M →Tp M is the tangent map. Let Gf n (R) ⊆ R[[x1 , . . . , xn ]] be the group of all formal diffeomorphisms of Rn , and Gf n (R)0 be the subgroup of all formal diffeomorphisms whose linear part has positive determinant

Borel’s Theorem for Diffeomorphisms. Let a finite-dimensional smooth manifold M of dimension n be given, p ∈ M and φ be a local chart around p such that φ(p) = 0. For each γ ∈ Diff c (M), let Tp∞ (γ) denote the Taylor series of φ ◦ γ ◦ φ−1 around 0. Then Tp∞ : Diff c (M)p,0 → Gf n (R)0 is a surjective homomorphism of Lie groups.
In this case, the surjectivity of Tp∞ : Diff c (Rn )p,0 → Gf n (R)0 has been established in Lemma 4.2. The Chain Rule for Taylor Polynomials entails that Tp∞ is a homomorphism of groups.

needs_review.question_text_raw: In [3], it is shown that the group Ghn(C) of germs of analytic diffeomorphisms around 0 in C^n is a regular Lie group in Milnor's sense. This answers the first half of [21, Problem VI.5] in the affirmative.

evidence.quote: In [3], it is shown that the group Ghn (C) of germs of analytic diffeomorphisms around 0 ∈ Cn (as first considered in [22]) is a regular Lie group in Milnor’s sense.1 This answers the first half of [21, Problem VI.5] in the affirmative.

needs_review.question_text_raw: Using a Frobenius theorem for co-Banach distributions, one obtains an existence result for integral subgroups, and hence [21, Problem VI.4] has an affirmative answer.

evidence.quote: Using a version of the Frobenius Theorem for co-Banach distributions on infinite-dimensional manifolds,2 one obtains the following result concerning integral subgroups in the sense of [21, Definition IV.4.7] (see [11]): Let G be a Lie group modelled on a locally convex space and h ⊆ L(G) be a Lie subalgebra such that L(G) = h ⊕ X for some Banach space X ⊆ L(G). Then there exists an integral subgroup H ⊆ G such that L(H) = h. Note that a complement X always exists if h has finite codimension. Hence [21, Problem VI.4] has an affirmative answer (even if G is not regular).
